newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Q3 seen robust but Q4 likely to be weak.
newsitem.headline: French Q3 seen robust but Q4 likely to be weak.

text.p: Figures due Thursday will show robust third-quarter French growth, boosted by a rush to buy cars ahead of the end to a state incentive scheme, but the fourth-quarter will be weak, economists said Wednesday.
"The big help in the third-quarter is going to come from households buying cars," said Steven Englander of Smith Barney in Paris, who expected growth of about one percent.
"When we get to the fourth quarter, the economy is going to be left to its own resources," Englander said.

The third-quarter GDP, due to be released at 0745 GMT, was expected to show a rise of 0.9 percent from the second quarter, according to a median forecast of 10 economists polled by Reuters. The range of forecasts was 0.7 percent to 1.3 percent.

Economists said the main boost to the third quarter would come from the scramble to buy cars ahead of the expiry of a subsidy scheme on September 30. The third quarter will also be flattered by a 0.4 percent fall in second quarter growth.
Further help could come from a favourable working day count during the summer when France's July 14 national holiday fell on a Sunday. Strong trade numbers are also seen contributing.
Barring any surprises, economists did not expect Thursday's figures to have an impact on financial markets, saying a strong rise was already priced in.
And they did not expect the Bank of France to cut rates following its monetary policy council meeting on Thursday -- especially given the latest controversy over France's strong franc policy.
"They won't cut rates with all the calls for an aggressive easing of the monetary stance," said David Naude of JP Morgan.
Former French president Valery Giscard D'Estaing renewed on Tuesday his call for a weaker franc, saying it would boost the sluggish economy.
A warning of the gloomier fourth quarter outlook came on Wednesday with figures showing consumer spending on manufactured goods fell a bigger-than-expected 2.6 percent in October.

Economists said not all of the fall could be explained by the plunge in car buying after the expiry of the subsidy scheme and that consumers remained cautious in the face of record unemployment of 12.6 percent.
"Everthing has been going down, consumer spending, industrial production -- there's not much momentum in the economy at this stage," said Naude.
Economists said they did not expect the truckers' strike, which has choked highway transportation across France for 10 days, to have any big impact on the fourth quarter.

The centre-right government has been banking on a revival in consumer spending and company investment to boost growth to 2.3 percent next year from 1.3 percent this year and help it cut the public deficit to qualify for European monetary union.
Economists said the economy was recovering but that the pace has been hampered by weak investment and continued destocking amid scepticism about future demand prospects.
"It is a very gentle recovery, weaker than other European recoveries," said Robert Prior of HSBC James Capel.

He saw the economy shrinking by 0.4 percent in the fourth quarter. He forecast the economy would grow by two percent in 1997, underperforming the European Union which he expected to show average 2.4 percent growth.

"The franc has remained strong on a trade-weighted basis, and the French economy is a little bit less sensitive to interest rate falls (than other countries) because of its strong net financial position," Prior said.
-- Penny MacRae, Paris Newsroom +33 1 4221 5452
